title: Choice modelling

definition.text: A family of methods that model how a person or group decides, using either their real choices or choices they state in a set context.

facts.text: It usually infers where items sit on a hidden scale, typically utility, from repeated choices of one option over another.
It is regarded as the best method for estimating willingness to pay for quality improvements that vary in several dimensions at once.
Its roots lie in Thurstone's 1920s research on food preferences and in random utility theory, which Daniel McFadden developed in economics.
McFadden used past transport choices to predict demand for the Bay Area Rapid Transit before it was built, work that earned him the 2000 Nobel economics prize.
A survey describes a good by attributes and levels; because full combinations explode, a phone with 2 brands, 3 shapes, 3 sizes and 4 memory options has 72, only a subset is shown.
It forces respondents to weigh trade-offs between attributes and lets analysts estimate implicit prices for each attribute.
In environmental economics, non-use values are usually estimated with stated preference methods such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.

notes: Terminology is disputed (choice-based conjoint vs discrete choice experiment) but this is naming, not a substantive debate.

definition.text: A revealed preference method that estimates the value of each characteristic of a good, such as a house, by breaking its price into contributions from its features.

facts.text: It is usually estimated with regression analysis and is used in real estate, environmental economics, marketing research and Consumer Price Index calculations.
In environmental work it measures how much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding other house features fixed.
A house is treated as a bundle of features, such as bedrooms, lot size and distance from the city centre, each given its own price.
Hedonic modelling was first published in the 1920s to value farm land, with roots also traced to Court's 1939 study of car prices.
Some critics argue its use in the US CPI can understate inflation, while studies abroad show non-hedonic methods can misstate inflation by ignoring quality change.

title: Replacement cost

definition.text: The amount one would have to pay at today's prices to replace an asset with an undamaged equivalent.

facts.text: It can differ from market value and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts depreciation.
Insurers use it as one way to value an insured item, such as paying the price of a similar new television today.
In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads matters because it can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

notes: Page is insurance-focused and never mentions valuing ecosystems by replacement cost; the replacement cost method for ecosystem services is a gap.

title: Revealed preference

definition.text: A way of working out what people prefer from the choices they actually make, pioneered by Paul Samuelson in 1938.

facts.text: It assumes people's preferences show in their purchasing habits.
It arose because utility, the satisfaction behind choices, could not be measured directly, so economists defined it from observed behaviour instead.
It contrasts with stated preference approaches, which ask people directly; economists usually trust revealed preferences more.
If bundle a is chosen when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b.
In ecosystem valuation, revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost link a service to a market good to estimate willingness to pay.
Critics say a purchase cannot show which alternatives were given up, and that the theory wrongly assumes preferences stay constant over time.

contested_note: Several economists, including Amartya Sen and Stanley Wong, criticise the theory as tautological or a failed research programme.

title: Weak axiom of revealed preference
article: Revealed preference#The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)

definition.text: A consistency rule saying that if a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable.

facts.text: The strong axiom (SARP) adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other, which preserves transitivity.
The generalised axiom (GARP) extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

definition.text: A 1967 result by Sydney Afriat proving that a finite set of observed choices satisfying GARP can be explained by a utility function.

facts.text: Its inequalities let the utility function be built directly from the data, unlike SARP, which only proves existence for infinite datasets.
It is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and build preferences from empirical data.
